meta.title: 2-1 vs. 3-2-1 Buydown: Payments, Subsidy & Note Rate
meta.heading: 2-1 vs. 3-2-1 Buydown: Payments, Subsidy & Note Rate
meta.description: Compare 2-1 and 3-2-1 buydowns on one fixed-rate loan. Separate borrower payments, subsidy funding and the payment after the subsidy ends.
meta.cardIntro: Compare the introductory borrower payments and the cash needed to fund them while keeping the principal, note rate and term fixed. The example isolates principal and interest; it does not assume a future refinance or determine loan-program eligibility.

mortgage-buydown.intro: Compare the introductory borrower payments and the cash needed to fund them while keeping the principal, note rate and term fixed. The example isolates principal and interest; it does not assume a future refinance or determine loan-program eligibility.
mortgage-buydown.answer: A 3-2-1 plan reduces the borrower’s early payment more deeply and for longer than a 2-1 plan, requiring more subsidy funding on the same loan. Both illustrations keep the 7% mortgage note rate and full lender payment unchanged. Compare the funding total and the eventual payment as well as the introductory amount.

sections.title: Does the loan interest rate actually change?
paragraphs: Separate three amounts: the borrower’s payment, the subsidy draw and the full payment credited to the loan. The note specifies the full obligation. A temporary agreement directs subsidy money to make up the difference during the introductory years. Calling the lower illustration a new contract interest rate gives the wrong balance and interest schedule.

Both the full payment and each reduced illustration use the original principal and original amortization term. Do not take the year-two remaining balance and amortize it at a new low rate over a shorter term. The accompanying calculator keeps a separate contract balance using the unchanged note rate and full lender P&I.

sections.title: How much subsidy funding does each plan need?
paragraphs: For each subsidized month, subtract borrower P&I from full contract P&I. Sum those differences for the plan. With the same note and term, 3-2-1 requires more funding than 2-1 because it adds a deeper first-year reduction. A 1-0 plan covers one year; 1-1 repeats a one-point reduction for two years.

The subsidy total is an upfront funding requirement, not a permanent reduction in contractual interest. A seller, lender or another eligible party may fund it under the applicable program and agreement. A dollar of funding cannot also be counted as an unrestricted closing credit without checking the actual offer.

sections.title: What payment should I budget after the subsidy ends?
paragraphs: For the example, both paths ultimately reach the same $1,995.91 monthly note-rate P&I. Add taxes, insurance, mortgage insurance, HOA dues and other recurring costs outside this worksheet. Those expenses may change even while P&I stays fixed. Review the scheduled payment increases before comparing the introductory amount with current rent.

Fannie Mae’s guide requires qualifying at the note rate within its covered program. Other loan rules and lender overlays must be checked separately. This worksheet does not determine approval or a maximum seller contribution. Future refinancing is a separate possibility, not an assumption that makes a later payment increase disappear.

sections.title: How is a temporary buydown different from discount points?
paragraphs: Permanent discount points change an offered note rate in exchange for an upfront price. A temporary buydown funds payment differences for a stated period without changing this model’s note rate. Compare complete offers, including principal, rate, points, fees, expected holding period and outstanding balance, using the mortgage comparison tool.

If a loan is repaid early, the agreement determines how unused subsidy funds are handled. Do not automatically subtract a projected refund from the total cost. The same applies to subsidy-account interest and servicing arrangements: they are outside the simple P&I funding model and need the actual contract.

sections.title: Compare two subsidy plans without changing the mortgage
paragraphs: Only the temporary subsidy plan changes. Both cases use the same $300,000 principal, 7% note rate and 360-month amortization. The lender payment and contract balance path are unchanged; the deeper reduction needs more upfront subsidy.

questions.question: Why can the 3-2-1 plan cost more even though its starting payment is lower?
questions.answer: The subsidy must cover a larger early payment gap and an additional reduced-payment year. Compare total funding, rather than treating the first-year payment as the full cost.

questions.question: Which payment should I use for the later household budget?
questions.answer: Use the unchanged note-rate principal and interest after the subsidy ends, plus separately estimated taxes, insurance and other housing costs. The introductory borrower amount is temporary.

questions.question: Can I compare a buydown with discount points using only the subsidy total?
questions.answer: No. A permanent rate offer changes the loan’s contractual rate. Compare the full offers, upfront charges, holding period and outstanding balance using consistent loan assumptions.

meta.title: Cash-Secured Put vs. Covered Call: Funding & Expiration Payoff
meta.heading: Cash-Secured Put vs. Covered Call: Funding & Expiration Payoff
meta.description: Compare matched cash-secured put and covered-call expiration scenarios. Inspect funding, capped gains, downside and the limits of payoff equivalence.
meta.cardIntro: The comparison starts with hypothetical positions entered at a $50 stock reference price, the same strike and share quantity, and matched net option receipts. It isolates expiration profit in dollars before comparing funding amounts or return percentages.

cash-secured-put.intro: The comparison starts with hypothetical positions entered at a $50 stock reference price, the same strike and share quantity, and matched net option receipts. It isolates expiration profit in dollars before comparing funding amounts or return percentages.
cash-secured-put.answer: Matched cash-secured puts and covered calls can show the same selected expiration profit in dollars while using different funding amounts and return denominators. In the controlled $50-entry, $50-strike, 200-share illustrations, either position loses $504 at a $45 stock price and earns at most $496. Actual premiums, financing and early-assignment behavior need not match.

sections.title: What cash or shares does each strategy require?
paragraphs: The cash-secured-put worksheet defines secured cash as strike price multiplied by total contract shares, before premium credit. At a $50 strike and 200 shares, that is $10,000. A broker may handle the premium, fees and buying power differently; this transparent denominator is not a margin requirement quote.

A covered call begins with shares plus a short call. Its profit calculation depends on the share purchase cost, call strike, premium, fees and any dividends explicitly included. The two positions can have similar expiration payoff shapes under matched assumptions, but different funding histories and operational risks. Do not compare percentages built from different denominators.

sections.title: How do I calculate the short put’s expiration outcome?
paragraphs: First multiply per-share premium by total shares, then subtract entered fees once. The example nets $496. At expiration, intrinsic obligation equals max(strike minus stock price, zero) times shares. Subtract that obligation from net premium. At $45, the $1,000 obligation leaves −$504.

If the stock finishes at or above the strike, the model retains $496 as its maximum profit. At a zero stock price, the economic loss is $10,000 minus $496, or $9,504. A price target is an assumption; the worksheet does not infer how likely either outcome is or recommend a particular underlying security.

sections.title: What does breakeven mean if shares are assigned?
paragraphs: Breakeven is strike minus net premium per share: $50 minus $496 divided by 200, or $47.52. This is the economic net acquisition cost before unentered costs and taxes. Assignment at the $50 strike can still produce an immediate economic loss if the shares are worth less than breakeven.

American-style options can be assigned before expiration. Expiration near the strike can involve exercise decisions and post-close price changes. The scenario table uses a simplified intrinsic-payoff assumption, not an execution promise. Adjusted contracts with cash or mixed-security deliverables need a different model; changing share multiplier alone is insufficient.

sections.title: When is a payoff comparison misleading?
paragraphs: For a meaningful comparison, align the strike, expiration horizon, share quantity, fee scope and stock-price scenarios. Use the actual stock entry cost for a covered call. Include dividends, interest on reserved cash and taxes only if both calculations treat them consistently. The calculator does not assume those omitted amounts cancel.

Net premium divided by secured cash is a one-trade ratio. Multiplying it into an annual rate would not account for losses, idle cash or changing option terms. This tool therefore displays the trade-period ratio without claiming a repeatable annual yield. Neither strategy removes substantial downside exposure to the underlying shares.

sections.title: Match the strike and fees before comparing expiration profit
paragraphs: Both hypothetical positions cover 200 shares at a $50 strike, receive $2.50 premium per share and incur $4 total opening option fees. The covered call also buys the shares at $50. No dividends, reserved-cash interest, taxes or exit charges are included. Equal dollar payoff in these selected cases does not establish equal real-world premiums, cash usage or early-assignment behavior.

questions.question: Why do these matched positions show the same selected expiration profit?
questions.answer: The chosen stock entry price equals the common strike, and net option receipts match. That makes their simplified expiration profit formulas coincide. Actual put and call quotes, financing and dividends need not match.

questions.question: Can I compare their percentage returns directly?
questions.answer: First check the denominators. The put worksheet uses full strike-based secured cash; the covered-call worksheet uses its positive net initial debit. Equal dollar profit can therefore produce different reported percentages.

questions.question: Does a matched expiration table mean the positions have identical risks before expiry?
questions.answer: No. Share ownership, dividend exposure, reserved-cash interest, trading costs and early exercise or assignment can differ. The table is a controlled expiration illustration, not an execution or suitability recommendation.

meta.title: Profitability Index vs. NPV: Formula, Timing & Project Size
meta.heading: Profitability Index vs. NPV: Formula, Timing & Project Size
meta.description: Compare PI and NPV for projects of different sizes using matched timing and discount rates. See why value per dollar and total value can rank differently.
meta.cardIntro: PI measures discounted future value per dollar of initial outlay; NPV measures the excess in dollars. Hold the timing and discount rate consistent before examining how project scale changes those two rankings.

profitability-index.intro: PI measures discounted future value per dollar of initial outlay; NPV measures the excess in dollars. Hold the timing and discount rate consistent before examining how project scale changes those two rankings.
profitability-index.answer: PI ranks discounted future value per dollar of initial outlay; NPV retains the dollar scale. In the one-year examples, the smaller project has the higher PI, while the larger project has the higher NPV. Neither comparison alone solves a constrained project-selection problem.

sections.title: Where does the initial investment go?
paragraphs: Enter the initial outlay as a positive denominator in its own field. In periodic mode, the first listed future cash flow occurs at the end of period one. Do not insert the initial outlay again as the first negative row. That would reduce the numerator and shift the intended timing of every flow.

Known-PV mode accepts a value that has already been discounted to the investment date. Dividing an undiscounted future receipt total by the outlay gives a different ratio. If you need a full irregular dated timeline, use the NPV calculator’s actual-date mode and preserve the same investment date and cash-flow definitions.

sections.title: How does payment spacing change PI?
paragraphs: Periodic mode uses an effective annual discount rate. Annual flows occur at years 1, 2 and so on; quarterly flows occur at 0.25, 0.5 and so on; monthly flows use twelfths of a year. The same three $4,000 amounts therefore have different present values if their spacing changes.

At 10% effective annual discounting, three annual $4,000 receipts have future PV of about $9,947.41. With a $10,000 outlay, PI is about 0.994741 and NPV is about −$52.59. The tool shows each discounted amount and varies the rate while retaining the same flows; it does not choose an appropriate rate.

sections.title: Why can PI and NPV rank projects differently?
paragraphs: Project A costs $1,000 and pays $1,500 in one year. At 10%, its future PV is $1,363.64, PI about 1.363636 and NPV $363.64. Project B costs $10,000 and pays $13,000 in one year: PV $11,818.18, PI about 1.181818 and NPV $1,818.18.

A creates more modeled present value per dollar invested, while B creates more modeled total net value. Which comparison matters depends on constraints and objectives outside this worksheet. A PI ranking alone is not a complete capital-allocation solution, especially with indivisible projects or different risk and timing assumptions.

sections.title: What if there are later negative cash flows?
paragraphs: This tool retains later net outflows in the future-value numerator. That convention preserves PI = 1 + NPV / initial outlay for the same inputs. Another benefit-cost convention divides the PV of all positive receipts by the PV of all outlays, including later ones; it can produce a different number.

For nonconventional flows, state the definition rather than treating the two ratios as interchangeable. Check taxes, terminal costs, inflation and discount-rate consistency. A PI above one only describes the entered model at that rate. It is not a guarantee, a financing approval or a recommendation to proceed with an investment.

sections.title: A higher PI can accompany a lower dollar NPV
paragraphs: Each project pays one hypothetical end-of-year receipt, discounted at 10%. Project A uses $1,000 initially and receives $1,500; Project B uses $10,000 and receives $13,000. These are separate project sizes, not a same-budget portfolio allocation or a complete capital-rationing solution.

table.caption: A higher PI can accompany a lower dollar NPV
rows: Project A: smaller initial outlay
Profitability index: 1.363636; Net present value: $363.64
One receipt at the end of year one; no intermediate cash flows.
Project B: larger initial outlay
Profitability index: 1.181818; Net present value: $1,818.18
One receipt at the end of year one; no intermediate cash flows.

questions.question: Which project does the larger PI identify in this example?
questions.answer: The smaller project delivers more discounted future net value per dollar initially invested. That ratio does not by itself identify the larger total dollar contribution.

questions.question: Why might NPV favor a different project?
questions.answer: NPV retains project scale. A lower value-per-dollar ratio applied to a much larger outlay can create more total discounted dollars.

questions.question: Can I choose a project using PI alone when capital is limited?
questions.answer: A ratio ranking is not a complete selection method when projects are indivisible, mutually exclusive or interdependent. Preserve budget constraints, timing and risk assumptions in a separate decision analysis.

meta.title: ROE & DuPont Analysis: Average Equity, Margin & Leverage
meta.heading: ROE & DuPont Analysis: Average Equity, Margin & Leverage
meta.description: Use DuPont factors to explain ROE changes. Compare the same income and assets with different book-equity denominators and inspect the leverage effect.
meta.cardIntro: Decompose ROE before treating a higher percentage as better operating performance. The paired cases keep net income, sales and average assets fixed and change only average book equity.

return-on-equity.intro: Decompose ROE before treating a higher percentage as better operating performance. The paired cases keep net income, sales and average assets fixed and change only average book equity.
return-on-equity.answer: ROE can rise without any increase in earnings. Holding income, sales and assets fixed while halving average equity doubles the equity multiplier and raises modeled ROE from 16% to 32%. The change identifies a denominator effect rather than an automatic operating improvement.

sections.title: Which equity balance belongs in ROE?
paragraphs: Use average book equity for the same period as income. If you only know beginning and ending equity, their arithmetic mean is a simple estimate. A large capital raise, buyback or restructuring during the period can make a time-weighted average more representative than the two endpoints.

Match the ownership scope as well. Common-shareholder earnings and common equity form one pair; another consistently defined total-equity pair may serve a different question. Do not divide consolidated income by an unrelated subsidiary’s equity, or replace book equity with market capitalization and call it the same accounting ROE.

sections.title: How do the three DuPont factors reconcile?
paragraphs: Net margin is income divided by sales. Asset turnover is sales divided by average assets. The equity multiplier is average assets divided by average equity. Multiplying them cancels sales and assets, leaving income divided by average equity, provided the denominators are defined and use matching periods.

In the example, $200,000 divided by $2 million is 10%; $2 million divided by $2.5 million is 0.8; $2.5 million divided by $1.25 million is 2. The product is 0.16, displayed as 16%. It is not 10 × 0.8 × 2 percent points added together. The worksheet shows direct ROE alongside the factor product.

sections.title: What if income or equity is negative?
paragraphs: A loss with positive average equity yields a negative ROE: −$200,000 on $1.25 million gives −16%. That is an interpretable loss ratio. Zero equity makes division undefined, while negative equity can turn a loss into a positive quotient that is easy to misread as strong performance.

The calculator suppresses the primary ratio when equity is nonpositive. Beginning/end mode also flags nonpositive endpoints even when their average is positive. With a known average alone, the tool cannot discover an intra-period crossing. Zero sales makes the margin and DuPont product unavailable, even when direct ROE still has a valid equity denominator.

sections.title: Does higher ROE always mean a better business?
paragraphs: No universal threshold is imposed. Higher leverage can raise the equity multiplier, and buybacks can shrink equity without improving operating performance. Compare margin, asset efficiency and financing together, with comparable businesses and periods. A single percentage does not measure every source of risk or value creation.

This worksheet reports the period you enter and does not automatically annualize quarterly income. Corporate ROE also differs from a rental owner’s cash yield on current property equity. Use the appropriate property tool for that task. None of these ratios by itself is a stock valuation, required return or investment recommendation.

sections.title: Changing equity alone changes ROE through the equity multiplier
paragraphs: Both cases use $200,000 net income, $2 million sales and $2.5 million average assets. Average book equity is $1.25 million in one illustration and $625,000 in the other. This isolates the arithmetic denominator effect; it is not a proposal to recapitalize a company or a full balance-sheet transaction model.

Return on equity: 16.00%; Equity multiplier: 2
Net income, sales and average assets remain fixed; only equity changes.
Average book equity $625,000

questions.question: Does doubling ROE here mean the company doubled its earnings?
questions.answer: No. Earnings are held fixed. The smaller equity denominator doubles the equity multiplier and the resulting ROE.

questions.question: Should I use market capitalization as the equity denominator?
questions.answer: Not for this accounting ROE measure. Use representative average book equity with the same ownership scope as the earnings numerator.

questions.question: Why inspect margin and asset turnover alongside ROE?
questions.answer: They separate profitability and asset efficiency from the equity multiplier. That helps reveal a leverage-driven ratio change instead of attributing every increase to operating improvement.

meta.title: 72(t) / SEPP Methods: Annual Amounts, Rates & Duration
meta.heading: 72(t) / SEPP Methods: Annual Amounts, Rates & Duration
meta.description: Compare first-year SEPP amounts from the RMD, fixed-amortization and annuitization methods. Separate payment arithmetic from qualification and series rules.
meta.cardIntro: Use the same dated single-life illustration to compare calculation methods, then assess the distribution arrangement separately. A computed annual amount does not establish a qualifying series or remove ordinary income tax.

72t.intro: Use the same dated single-life illustration to compare calculation methods, then assess the distribution arrangement separately. A computed annual amount does not establish a qualifying series or remove ordinary income tax.
72t.answer: The RMD, fixed-amortization and fixed-annuitization methods produce different first-year amounts under the same dated single-life assumptions. Compare those amounts without treating the largest payment as a recommendation or a qualifying arrangement. Ordinary income tax and the ongoing series requirements remain separate.

sections.title: How do the three methods differ?
paragraphs: The RMD method divides the relevant account balance by a permitted life-expectancy factor for the distribution year. In this single-life worksheet, age means age on the owner’s birthday in that calendar year. The first estimate uses the prior December 31 balance; later annual amounts require new balances and age factors rather than freezing the first output.

Fixed amortization divides the selected initial balance by the present-value factor for level annual payments over Single Life expectancy. Fixed annuitization uses survival probabilities from the regulation’s mortality table instead. Both fixed methods keep the initially determined annual amount under their rules. A life-expectancy period is not a substitute for an annuity factor.

sections.title: Can I reproduce the IRS age-50 example?
paragraphs: The IRS example uses $400,000, Single Life expectancy of 36.2 and a 4% selected rate for the fixed methods. RMD-method division gives about $11,049.72. Amortization gives about $21,101.63. Our mortality-weighted annuity-immediate factor is about 18.15678885 and produces about $22,030.33, matching the IRS whole-dollar illustrations.

The annuity calculation weights a year-end $1 by the probability of surviving to that payment and discounts it at the selected annual rate. The finite sum runs through terminal age 120, which is explicitly disclosed. The worksheet does not use an annuity-due first payment, substitute a pre-2022 mortality table or forecast the owner’s actual longevity.

sections.title: Which interest rate may I enter?
paragraphs: For the two fixed methods, the selected rate cannot exceed the greater of 5% and the qualifying 120% federal mid-term rate for either of the two months immediately before the first payment month. The baseline therefore permits a selected rate up to 5% without entering a higher monthly figure. RMD-method division does not use this interest rate.

If using a higher ceiling, enter the IRS-published 120% figure for the appropriate month, not the unmultiplied base AFR. The tool displays which two months correspond to the chosen start date but does not fetch or authenticate your historical rate inputs. This calculation rate is separate from any future investment-return assumption. No portfolio-growth forecast is required here.

sections.title: When can a series change, and what remains outside the model?
paragraphs: The general duration compares the fifth anniversary of the first payment with the date age 59½ is reached. The later milestone matters; it is not simply five calendar years or the fifth annual payment. A permitted one-time move from a fixed method to RMD in a later distribution year does not erase that original duration requirement.

Account additions, extra withdrawals and certain transfers can modify a series and trigger additional tax and interest. Income tax may still apply even when an early-distribution exception applies. Confirm account selection, valuation, installment totals, rounding and any partial first year with the custodian or qualified tax professional. A monthly budget equivalent and a date milestone are not instructions to begin or stop a distribution.

sections.title: Compare first-year methods with the same account illustration
paragraphs: The illustration uses a person born August 15, 1973, a December 1, 2023 series start and an entered December 31, 2022 balance of $400,000. Fixed methods use an illustrative 4% rate with no prior-month AFR values supplied. These are historical model inputs, not a current rate recommendation or confirmation that the valuation date is eligible.

questions.question: Does the largest displayed payment identify the best method?
questions.answer: No. A first-year amount does not evaluate spending needs, taxes, account resilience or compliance with an ongoing series. Those questions require the actual circumstances and applicable rules.

questions.question: Is the RMD calculation method here the same as being subject to ordinary required distributions?
questions.answer: No. It is the life-expectancy calculation method used for this SEPP illustration. The example’s method label does not establish an ordinary age-based required distribution.

questions.question: Does selecting a fixed rate validate a SEPP arrangement?
questions.answer: No. Permitted-rate selection, account and valuation rules, payment handling and later modifications remain separate requirements. Check the IRS guidance and the actual arrangement before relying on a withdrawal plan.
